title: Foundational Skills for Older Readers: What the Research Actually Says
author: Secondary Literacy Commons
summary: The Secondary Literacy Commons recaps a conversation with Dr. Sarah Lupo, a James Madison University reading researcher and high school reading specialist, on what research says about developing foundational literacy skills in older students. Lupo opens with a critical frame: comprehension is always the goal; foundational instruction (decoding, morphology, fluency) exists in service of that goal. She uses a daisy-picking metaphor to explain that all readers who understand a passage—whether they grasp one inference or five—have achieved comprehension; instruction should extend the range of what each reader picks up. The article addresses common misconceptions about adolescent literacy, including the false belief that older students who lack automaticity simply need more practice reading. Instead, Lupo emphasizes targeted, explicit instruction in morphology and fluency that is embedded in meaningful texts and always connected back to comprehension.
points: Comprehension is always the goal: foundational skills instruction at the secondary level must be situated as a means to comprehension, never treated as a discrete skill set divorced from meaning-making.

Older students with weak automaticity need explicit instruction, not more independent reading: unsupported reading practice for students who lack fluency reinforces inefficient decoding rather than correcting it.
Morphology instruction is high-leverage at the secondary level: Latin and Greek root knowledge unlocks academic vocabulary across content areas, providing multiplicative returns on instruction time.

The daisy metaphor reframes differentiation: all students who understand a text are comprehending—instruction should extend the range of inferences and details each student picks up, not decide who is a 'real reader.'
Fluency at the secondary level is often invisible as a need: teachers who mistake slow, halting reading for an engagement problem may miss the decoding automaticity deficits underneath.
quotes: Sarah opened with a reminder that can get lost when the conversation turns to decoding and fluency: comprehension is the goal. Always. Everything else—morphology, word reading, fluency instruction—exists in service of that.

She offered a metaphor that landed for the group. Think of comprehension like a field of daisies. Some students walk through and pick one. Some pick a few. Some pick a handful. All three understood the passage—just at different depths.
We cannot assume that older students who struggle with fluency will simply grow out of it through exposure. They need explicit, targeted instruction delivered with intention.
What we know about morphology is that it's one of the highest-leverage things we can teach at the secondary level. One root can unlock dozens of academic words across multiple content areas.
The goal is always to bring students back to meaning. Foundational skills instruction that never connects to comprehension is practicing a fire drill that never serves in a real fire.
